#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Current Employment Statistics (CES)
Description: The Current Employment Statistics (CES) program is a monthly survey conducted by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The survey provides employment, hours, and earnings estimates based on payroll records of business establishments.
URL: https://bls.gov/ces

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Current Employment Statistics (CES): research and preservation report

**Research date:** October 8–9, 2026  
**Primary publisher:** U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), U.S. Department of Labor  
**Official national program website:** https://www.bls.gov/ces/

## Executive summary

Your title, description, and URL are substantially correct. The important refinements are:

- **CES is a statistical program and a family of datasets**, not one fixed downloadable file.
- It surveys **businesses and government agencies**, using establishment payroll records to estimate **nonfarm payroll employment, paid hours, and earnings by industry**.
- The supplied URL is specifically the **national CES program**. Related state and metropolitan-area estimates are published through [State and Metro Area Employment, Hours, and Earnings](https://www.bls.gov/sae/).
- CES counts **payroll jobs, not unique employed people**. Someone employed by two establishments can be counted twice.
- CES does **not** produce the national unemployment rate. That comes from the separate Current Population Survey (CPS).
- Published CES data are free, machine-readable, and public domain. Identifiable employer responses are confidential.
- The greatest preservation challenge is **revision and versioning**: a historical value downloaded today may differ from the value published when that month first appeared.

CES is exceptionally important public statistical infrastructure. It informs monetary and fiscal policy, recession analysis, wage negotiations, business planning, journalism, and numerous other economic datasets. Preserving only the latest numerical series would lose evidence of what policymakers and the public knew at earlier dates.

**Suggested corrected catalog description:**

> The Current Employment Statistics program of the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics produces monthly estimates of nonfarm payroll employment, paid hours, and earnings by industry from a survey of business and government establishments. National estimates cover payroll jobs located in the 50 states and the District of Columbia; related state and metropolitan-area estimates are published separately. Estimates undergo monthly revisions, annual employment benchmarking, and seasonal-adjustment revisions.

Sources: [CES overview](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesprog.htm), [CES frequently asked questions](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesfaq.htm), [concepts](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/concepts.htm).

---

## 1. Dataset identity, ownership, and institutional setting

| Attribute | Findings |
|---|---|
| Common title | Current Employment Statistics |
| Other names | Establishment survey; payroll survey; Employment, Hours, and Earnings |
| National program designation | CES-N |
| Related subnational program | CES-State and Area, or CES-SA |
| Publisher and principal steward | Bureau of Labor Statistics, Department of Labor |
| Institutional structure | Federal-state statistical program, involving state labor-market information agencies |
| Respondents | Businesses and government agencies reporting establishment payroll information |
| Public product | Aggregate statistical estimates and derived time series—not employer-level payroll records |
| Main frequency | Monthly; selected quarterly averages and annual averages also available |
| Industry classification | Currently based on the 2022 North American Industry Classification System, or NAICS |
| National database abbreviation | `CE` |
| Geography | National estimates cover the 50 states and District of Columbia; Puerto Rico and U.S. Virgin Islands are excluded from national totals |
| Principal release | *The Employment Situation*, alongside separate CPS results |

The national and state/area programs share the survey sample and collection infrastructure, but their estimation, benchmarking, publication detail, and release schedules are not identical. They should be cataloged as related products rather than treated as interchangeable files.

CES estimates are primarily **workplace-based**. They measure employment where establishments are located, not where workers reside. That matters when comparing CES with resident employment, commuting patterns, or local unemployment.

Sources: [sample design](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/design.htm), [CES FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesfaq.htm), [historical Handbook chapter](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/pdf/ces-20110307.pdf).

### Contact

BLS’s national CES contact file lists:

- **Email:** cesinfo@bls.gov
- **Telephone:** 202-691-6555
- **Industry analyst availability:** 8:30 a.m.–4:30 p.m. Eastern Time

Source: [official CES contact file](https://download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/ce/ce.contacts).

---

## 2. Legal authority, mandate, and confidentiality

### A. A specific monthly publication mandate

CES is supported by more than a general agency mission. **29 U.S.C. § 2** directs BLS to collect, collate, report, and publish, **at least monthly**, statistics on the volume of and changes in employment, including:

- Number of persons employed;
- Total wages paid;
- Total hours of employment;
- Employment in federal, state, and local government and specified industries;
- Geographic detail by states and other subdivisions prescribed by the Secretary of Labor.

The statute also authorizes cooperative arrangements with federal, state, and municipal agencies.

**Important distinction:** this is a mandate to BLS to produce statistics. It does not make every employer’s response compulsory under federal law.

Source: [29 U.S.C. § 2, official U.S. Code](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=%28title%3A29+section%3A2+edition%3Aprelim%29).

### B. Federal participation is voluntary; some jurisdictions require reporting

BLS describes CES participation as **voluntary under federal law**.

Its respondent FAQ lists mandatory reporting in **California, New Mexico, Ohio, Oregon, South Carolina, and Puerto Rico**, with the South Carolina requirement applying to firms with more than 20 employees.

However, BLS pages are not completely synchronized: the general CES FAQ omits Ohio, and an archived methods chapter lists fewer jurisdictions. For compliance decisions, consult the current survey form and underlying state statute rather than relying on an older descriptive page.

Sources: [respondent FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/respondents/ces/faqs.htm), [general CES FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesfaq.htm), [archived data-source documentation](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/archive/20250207/data.htm).

### C. Paperwork Reduction Act oversight

The collection is identified as:

- **OMB control number:** `1220-0011`
- **Collection title:** *Report on Current Employment Statistics*

The approval record is valuable documentation of questionnaires, reporting burden, methodological justification, changes, and public-comment procedures. An OMB-record mirror reports an expiration of August 31, 2027; approval status should be checked against the official record when used operationally.

Sources: [official information-collection record](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202503-1220-001), [OMB-record mirror and document inventory](https://omb.report/omb/1220-0011).

### D. Confidentiality protections

BLS pledges to use respondent information for statistical purposes and not disclose identifiable responses without informed consent, subject to applicable law. Its CES methods documentation cites the **Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act (CIPSEA)** and other federal protections.

Published estimates undergo disclosure and sample-adequacy tests. BLS states that details of those tests are confidential.

Consequences for researchers:

- Public downloads do not contain identifiable establishment payroll records.
- Public time series cannot support arbitrary employer-level linkage.
- Published cells can disappear or be combined because of confidentiality or quality concerns.
- A claim that a public series is missing should distinguish **suppression**, **discontinuation**, **reclassification**, and **ordinary collection gaps**.

For employer-level research, contact BLS’s [Restricted Data Access program](https://www.bls.gov/rda/). This report does not establish the current eligibility or availability of a particular CES microdata extract.

Source: [CES confidentiality and data-source documentation](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/archive/20250207/data.htm).

---

## 3. What CES measures—and what it does not

### Reference period

Employment refers to employees who received pay for any part of the **pay period containing the 12th day of the month**.

This is not a count taken on the last day of the month, nor a count of everyone who worked at some point during the entire calendar month.

### Coverage and exclusions

CES includes full-time and part-time payroll employees, including salaried corporate officers. Government coverage is civilian.

Major exclusions include:

- Farm workers;
- Sole proprietors and unincorporated self-employed workers;
- Unpaid family workers and volunteers;
- Private-household domestic workers;
- Military personnel;
- Certain intelligence-agency employees specified by BLS.

A person with jobs at two establishments can contribute two jobs to the total. CES is therefore not a full-time-equivalent measure or a unique-person count.

### Main measures

| Measure | Meaning and cautions |
|---|---|
| All employees | Payroll job count; commonly published in thousands |
| Production and nonsupervisory employees | A subset defined differently across industry groups; not an occupational classification |
| Women employees | Industry employment counts; not a comprehensive demographic dataset |
| Average weekly hours | Average paid hours, including relevant paid leave |
| Average hourly earnings | Payroll divided by paid hours; not a wage-rate schedule or median wage |
| Average weekly earnings | Derived from average hourly earnings and average weekly hours |
| Manufacturing overtime hours | Overtime hours collected for manufacturing |
| Aggregate hours and payrolls | Derived measures useful for economic activity analysis |
| Indexes | Aggregate hours/payroll indexes and employment diffusion indexes |
| Real earnings | Constant-dollar earnings series requiring attention to the deflator and base period |

Hours and earnings estimates are for **private-sector employees**, whereas employment estimates also cover government.

### Paid hours are not strictly hours worked

CES paid-hours reporting includes work hours, overtime, and qualifying employer-paid holidays, vacations, sick leave, and other leave. It therefore differs from a pure hours-worked measure.

### Earnings are not total compensation

Payroll is measured before employee deductions and includes regular pay and specified premium or recurring payments. It excludes employer-paid benefits, irregular bonuses, retroactive payments, and payments in kind. Tips are included under the relevant CES payroll definition.

Average earnings can change because the mix of jobs changes. For example, losing many low-paid jobs can raise average hourly earnings even if no remaining employee receives a raise.

Sources: [CES concepts](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/concepts.htm), [CES FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesfaq.htm), [flat-file documentation](https://download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/ce/ce.txt).

---

## 4. Collection, sampling, and estimation

### Sample scale

The general BLS FAQ describes approximately **119,000 businesses and government agencies representing 629,000 worksites**. The flat-file documentation describes approximately **119,000 organizations and 622,000 worksites**.

These are approximate, changing descriptions—not a permanently fixed sample size. Businesses, UI accounts, employer units, and physical worksites are different counting units. Preserve the source date whenever quoting sample size.

### Sampling frame and design

The principal sampling frame is BLS’s longitudinal employer database, constructed from the **Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW)**.

Private-sector sample design is stratified by:

- State;
- Industry;
- Employment size.

Works sites are clustered by unemployment-insurance account number. Sampling allocation aims to improve precision within available resources. Large and other designated certainty units are included with a weight of one.

Government employment uses a different approach: coverage is sufficiently extensive that BLS does not apply the same probability-sample design used for private establishments.

### Collection methods

BLS collects reports through electronic data interchange, secure web reporting, computer-assisted telephone interviewing, and other methods. Payroll-processing firms can transmit information for multiple establishments.

Reports undergo validation and editing before estimation.

### Employment estimation

The core national employment estimator moves the previous month’s estimate forward using the employment change among weighted, matched reporting establishments. It then adds an adjustment for employment associated with business births and deaths not captured promptly by the sample.

Some small national industry domains use model-based estimation. Users should retain series-specific documentation rather than assume every published cell has identical estimation properties.

Sources: [design](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/design.htm), [calculation](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/calculation.htm), [CES FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesfaq.htm).

### Birth–death modeling

New establishments enter administrative records with a lag; closed establishments may stop reporting. A current survey cannot immediately observe all these changes.

CES uses a two-stage adjustment:

1. A sample treatment that offsets part of missing business-birth employment with employment associated with business deaths.
2. A modeled residual informed by QCEW history.

**Do not subtract a published birth–death component directly from the seasonally adjusted headline job change.** Birth–death forecasts are added to **not-seasonally-adjusted** estimates, which are then seasonally adjusted.

### Significant 2026 change

Beginning with preliminary January 2026 estimates, BLS modified the model-based birth–death component to incorporate **current sample information**. It also applied the modification to the recalculated post-benchmark months and November–December 2025.

BLS says persistent, relatively large birth–death forecast errors since the 2020 benchmark motivated changes. This is an important methodological event to document in longitudinal research.

Sources: [birth–death model](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesbd.htm), [birth–death FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesbdqa.htm).

---

## 5. Publication, revisions, benchmarking, and uncertainty

### Release timing

Preliminary national estimates are published in *The Employment Situation*, generally early in the following month at **8:30 a.m. Eastern Time**. The exact date varies; use the [BLS release calendar](https://www.bls.gov/schedule/news_release/) rather than assuming “first Friday” is universal.

Detailed industry series may have different publication timing from the initial headline release.

### Monthly revision sequence

Ordinarily, an observation passes through:

1. **First preliminary estimate**;
2. **Second preliminary estimate**, the following month;
3. **Third, final sample-based estimate**, another month later.

Additional reports and updated seasonal adjustment contribute to revisions.

“Final sample-based” does **not** mean permanently final.

### Annual employment benchmarking

CES employment estimates are annually realigned to a more comprehensive March employment count:

- About **97%** of employment within CES scope is covered by unemployment-insurance administrative records.
- The remaining employment is benchmarked using other sources, including Railroad Retirement Board and County Business Patterns information.

BLS adjusts preceding months and recalculates subsequent estimates. Hours and earnings are **not directly benchmarked to an equivalent administrative census**, although annual processing can revise them.

Benchmarking is normally incorporated with the January estimates released in February. Approximately five years of seasonally adjusted history are revisited annually, and reconstructions can reach further back.

BLS notes that it can take nearly **two years** before not-seasonally-adjusted estimates are considered final, with further changes still possible after reclassification or error correction.

Sources: [calculation and benchmarking](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/calculation.htm), [CES FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesfaq.htm).

### Example: the March 2025 benchmark incorporated in February 2026

BLS’s benchmark article reports a downward revision of **898,000 jobs, or 0.6%, to the seasonally adjusted March 2025 total nonfarm employment level**.

This was a revision to an employment **level**, not a statement that 898,000 jobs were lost during one month.

The example demonstrates why archived first releases and current revised history serve different research purposes.

Source: [national benchmark article](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesbmart.htm).

### Seasonal adjustment

CES uses concurrent seasonal adjustment with Census Bureau **X-13ARIMA-SEATS** software. Models and factors address recurring seasonal patterns and selected calendar effects.

Preserve both adjusted and unadjusted series:

- Seasonally adjusted data are generally better for interpreting short-term movement.
- Unadjusted data retain the observed seasonal pattern and are necessary for examining birth–death components and many benchmarking questions.

Some series are independently seasonally adjusted and are not used to aggregate higher-level totals; BLS identifies these with footnotes.

### Reliability and uncertainty

CES is subject to:

- Sampling error;
- Reporting and processing error;
- Nonresponse bias;
- Sampling-frame imperfections;
- Model error;
- Errors in administrative benchmark inputs.

BLS publishes standard errors and relative standard errors. Confidence intervals based on sampling variance do **not** capture every source of error.

For a 90% interval, BLS illustrates using an estimate ± **1.645 times its standard error**. A small monthly change may not be statistically distinguishable from zero.

### Collection rate is not response rate

BLS’s collection rate measures receipts from the active reporting sample at an estimation deadline. Its response rate includes refusals and has a different denominator and unit basis.

A high collection rate should not be interpreted as the share of all initially selected employers participating.

Sources: [reliability methods](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/calculation.htm), [CES FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesfaq.htm).

---

## 6. History and changes affecting comparability

CES dates to **October 1915**, initially covering four manufacturing industries with employment and payroll change statistics.

| Period | Development |
|---|---|
| 1915–1920s | Initial manufacturing survey; early state cooperation; rapid expansion of industry coverage |
| 1930s | Great Depression-era expansion; hours and earnings collection; first benchmarking to manufacturing census data |
| 1935 onward | Unemployment-insurance reporting created a major future administrative benchmark source |
| 1940 | First UI-based national benchmark |
| 1949 | Cooperative agreements covered all 48 states |
| 1954 | BLS began publishing seasonally adjusted estimates |
| 1960s | Expanded sampling requirements and collection of women employment and production/nonsupervisory hours and earnings |
| 1979 | Levitan Commission criticized aspects of sample design, benchmarking, documentation, and coverage and recommended improvements |
| 1982 | Consistent annual UI-based benchmarking began |
| 1980s–1990s | Service-sector expansion, automated collection, electronic reporting, and methodological review |
| 2000–2003 | Implementation of private-sector probability sampling |
| 2003 | Conversion from SIC to NAICS, birth–death modeling, concurrent seasonal adjustment, and historical reconstruction |
| 2006–2008 | All-employee hours/payroll collection began; experimental estimates followed |
| Early 2010s | Official all-employee hours and earnings became established |
| 2015 | Transition to X-13ARIMA-SEATS |
| 2020–2021 | Temporary pandemic-related estimation adjustments |
| 2023 | Adoption of NAICS 2022 |
| 2025–2026 | Changes to birth–death modeling incorporating more current sample information |

Sources: [BLS program history](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/history.htm), [centennial sample-design history](https://www.bls.gov/opub/mlr/2016/article/one-hundred-years-of-current-employment-statistics-sample-design.htm), [2026 model FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesbdqa.htm).

### Available history is not the same as program age

- Current high-level employment series extend to **1939**.
- Most detailed industry employment series begin around **1990**.
- All-employee hours and earnings series begin in **2006**.
- Discontinued SIC-based series can extend further back, in some cases to 1919.

Do not concatenate SIC and NAICS series without a documented concordance and comparability assessment.

### A notable public-interest intervention

BLS records that it discontinued women-worker series in 2006, then reinstated them in 2007 after **more than 5,000 complaint letters**. Plans to drop production and nonsupervisory series were also shelved.

This is a concrete example of users influencing the preservation of statistical coverage—not merely accessing an already completed product.

### Historical methodological scrutiny

BLS’s history documents investigations and reviews following allegations of political manipulation, including the 1962 Gordon Committee and a 1993 GAO review. It reports that those reviews dismissed the allegations while methodological improvement remained important.

That historical finding should not be generalized into a claim about every later controversy.

---

## 7. Typical users and benefits to the public

### Documented users

| User | Uses |
|---|---|
| Federal Reserve | Labor-market assessment, monetary policy, industrial production inputs |
| Bureau of Economic Analysis | Wage and salary estimates used in personal income statistics |
| National Bureau of Economic Research | Evidence for business-cycle turning points |
| Federal, state, and local officials | Tax-revenue forecasting, budgeting, fiscal-policy analysis |
| Other BLS programs | Inputs to JOLTS, productivity, compensation, and subnational labor-market statistics |
| Businesses and trade associations | Demand assessment, industry analysis, forecasting, investment and staffing plans |
| Labor unions | Wage negotiations and industry employment analysis |
| Researchers and universities | Macroeconomic, labor-market, industry, and historical research |
| Financial-market participants | Economic forecasting and investment decisions |
| Journalists and educators | Public explanation of economic conditions |

Sources: [uses and major users](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/archive/20230906/presentation.htm), [CES contributions as economic indicators](https://www.bls.gov/opub/mlr/2016/article/current-employment-statistics-data-and-their-contributions-as-key-economic-indicators.htm).

### Public benefits

1. **Timely economic visibility.** CES provides an early indication of contraction, recovery, and sectoral change.
2. **A common factual reference.** Government, labor, businesses, and citizens can examine the same publicly accessible statistics.
3. **Better-informed policy.** Employment, hours, and earnings help assess demand and income conditions.
4. **Industry-level accountability.** Aggregate national growth can be separated into industries with different trajectories.
5. **Long historical context.** Users can compare current conditions with earlier recessions and structural shifts.
6. **Statistical infrastructure.** Improvements or disruptions in CES propagate into many other economic measures.
7. **Low-cost reuse.** Free bulk files and an API enable independent analysis without purchasing a commercial feed.

These benefits are not proof that any particular policy is effective. CES describes outcomes; causal evaluation requires additional methods and evidence.

## 8. Access, formats, identifiers, and rights

### Principal access routes

| Route | Best suited to |

| [CES databases](https://www.bls.gov/ces/data/) | Interactive discovery and selected-series retrieval |
| [CES bulk directory](https://download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/ce/) | Large-scale analysis and preservation |

| [Benchmark article archive](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesbmkarch.htm) | Annual revisions and methodological context |
| [State/area program](https://www.bls.gov/sae/) | Subnational products |

### Bulk data and metadata

The national directory includes:

- `ce.data.0.AllCESSeries` — current published series and their historical observations;
- Industry- and measure-specific subsets;
- `ce.series` — series titles, codes, footnotes, and start/end periods;
- `ce.industry`;
- `ce.datatype`;
- `ce.supersector`;
- `ce.seasonal`;
- `ce.period`;
- `ce.footnote`;
- `ce.txt` — documentation;
- `ce.contacts`.

The files are tab-delimited text. A typical observation has:

```text
series_id    year    period    value    footnote_codes
```

**Preserve actual headers and code tables.** Documentation can lag implementation; do not build a parser solely from a prose field-width description.

### Useful example identifiers

| Series ID | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `CES0000000001` | Total nonfarm employment, seasonally adjusted, thousands |
| `CEU0000000001` | Total nonfarm employment, not seasonally adjusted, thousands |
| `CES0500000003` | Total private average hourly earnings, all employees, seasonally adjusted |

In standard national identifiers, `CE` identifies the database and `S`/`U` distinguishes adjusted/unadjusted series.

Period codes `M01`–`M12` identify calendar months. **`M13` means annual average**, not a thirteenth month. Some derived products have other period conventions.

Sources: [file documentation](https://download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/ce/ce.txt), [series catalog](https://download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/ce/ce.series).

### API capabilities and limits

BLS’s API FAQ lists:

| Limit | Registered access | Unregistered access |
|---|---:|---:|
| Daily queries | 500 | 25 |
| Series per query | 50 | 25 |
| Years per query | 20 | 10 |
| Rate limit | 50 requests per 10 seconds | Same |

The API returns observations and footnotes; registered version-2 features include selected descriptive and calculation options. A returned JSON observation is an aggregate published estimate, **not raw respondent data**.

Use bulk files for comprehensive acquisition rather than thousands of small API calls. Check current limits before deployment.

Sources: [API FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/developers/api_faqs.htm), [version-2 signatures](https://www.bls.gov/developers/api_signature_v2.htm).

BLS states that its published material is public domain, except previously copyrighted photographs and illustrations. It requests source attribution. Its emblem is a protected trademark.

For CES numerical data:

- No special permission is needed for reuse;
- Redistribution and derivative analysis are permitted;
- Cite BLS and distinguish your transformations from its published estimates;
- Do not imply BLS endorsement.

Source: [BLS copyright policy](https://www.bls.gov/opub/copyright-information.htm).

## 9. Preservation assessment and recommended archival package

**Assessment: very high preservation priority.**

CES has unusually strong historical, policy, and downstream statistical significance. The main risk is not simply losing a website: it is losing **earlier versions, classifications, documentation, and discontinued series**.

### A. Preserve versions, not just historical dates

A file containing observations from 1939 onward is not necessarily an archive of every release since 1939. It generally contains the **currently published historical estimates**.

Use a preservation key such as:

```text
publisher + product + series_id + reference_period + release/vintage_date
```

The release date and reference month are different dimensions.

### B. Capture at every release

Recommended capture:

- Complete national bulk data;
- Series and mapping files;
- API responses for key headline series;
- Employment Situation release in available HTML, text, and PDF forms;
- Detailed CES tables;
- Collection and response rates;
- Birth–death components;
- Revision tables;
- Release calendar and change notices.

### C. Capture annual processing separately

Preserve:

- Benchmark articles and tables;
- Preliminary versus final benchmark announcements;
- Seasonal-adjustment documentation and available specifications;
- New/discontinued-series lists;
- NAICS revisions, crosswalks, and reconstruction notes;
- Error corrections.

### D. Preserve the wider documentation

The archive should include:

- All CES Handbook of Methods chapters and available historical editions;
- Questionnaires and respondent instructions;
- OMB supporting statements and approvals;
- Statutory authority;
- Confidentiality and publication standards;
- Methodological research papers;
- Federal-state program documentation;
- Contact information.

### E. Technical preservation practices

These are recommendations, not assertions about BLS’s internal archive:

- Retain original downloaded bytes alongside normalized CSV or Parquet.
- Record source URL, retrieval timestamp, release date, file size, and SHA-256 checksum.
- Save a manifest identifying all acquired and missing files.
- Store HTTP metadata where available.
- Preserve footnotes as structured data.
- Capture web pages and dependencies in WARC where feasible.
- Keep immutable release snapshots; do not overwrite earlier files.
- Maintain redundant copies and periodic fixity checks.
- Test that series metadata can still be joined to observations.
- Assign persistent repository identifiers to deposited snapshots.

### F. Funding disruptions can create real gaps

The current flat-file documentation explicitly notes missing **October 2025 real earnings data** and certain collection-rate values due to the 2025 lapse in appropriations.

Archive such explanations. Do not silently interpolate missing observations or confuse a missing initial publication with a permanently missing employment estimate.

Source: [CES flat-file documentation](https://download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/ce/ce.txt).

### G. No verified retention guarantee

This research did not establish a CES-specific records-retention schedule, guaranteed permanent storage location, or complete official archive of every historical estimate vintage.

A preservationist should ask BLS directly about:

- Retention of monthly production snapshots;
- Availability of historical machine-readable vintages;
- Coverage of discontinued databases;
- Applicable records schedules and archival transfer arrangements.

## 10. Guidance for data scientists and policy analysts

### Essential analytical safeguards

1. **Choose the right concept.** Payroll jobs are not unique people, job openings, hires, or full-time equivalents.
2. **Use one consistent vintage for ordinary historical analysis.** Mixing snapshots can manufacture changes that never appeared in any single release.
3. **Use contemporaneous vintages for real-time forecasting or policy reconstruction.** Revised data introduce look-ahead bias.
4. **Retain units.** Employment commonly appears in thousands; earnings in dollars; indexes have measure-specific bases.
5. **Do not mix adjusted and unadjusted observations.**
6. **Do not double-count industry hierarchies.** Parent industries and their components overlap.
7. **Do not average earnings series unweighted.** Appropriate aggregation requires payroll/hours or other relevant weights.
8. **Treat missing values as missing, not zero.**
9. **Retain preliminary and independent-adjustment flags.**
10. **Account for NAICS and geographic changes.**
11. **Use uncertainty information.** Small industry movements may be noise.
12. **Distinguish net employment change from gross job creation and destruction.**
13. **Do not infer policy causality from a before/after chart alone.**

### Limitations relevant to policy activism

CES cannot by itself answer:

- Whether racial or ethnic employment gaps widened;
- Whether the typical worker received a raise;
- Whether jobs provide benefits or predictable schedules;
- Whether residents of a neighborhood gained employment;
- Whether contractors or self-employed gig workers benefited;
- Whether observed growth was caused by a particular policy.

Average earnings are not median earnings, and women employment counts do not make CES a complete inequality dataset.

### Useful complementary sources

| Question | Complementary source |
|---|---|
| Unemployment, labor-force participation, worker demographics | Current Population Survey |
| County-level administrative employment and wages | QCEW |
| Occupations and occupational pay | Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics |
| Hires, openings, quits, layoffs | JOLTS |
| Gross job gains and losses | Business Employment Dynamics |
| Benefits and employer compensation costs | National Compensation Survey, ECEC, ECI |
| Resident-based local unemployment | Local Area Unemployment Statistics |
| Income and residential characteristics | American Community Survey |

These products have different universes, reference periods, definitions, and revision processes. Link them conceptually before linking them mechanically.

### Public accountability priorities

A sound monitoring agenda would track:

- Survey response and collection rates separately;
- Revision magnitude and persistence;
- Birth–death model performance;
- Losses of publication detail;
- Timeliness and funding disruptions;
- Accessibility of metadata and historical versions;
- Changes in confidentiality or publication practices.

Revision is part of responsible statistical production; its mere existence is not evidence of manipulation. Conversely, transparent explanation of unusually large revisions is a legitimate public-interest expectation.

Record at minimum:

## Overall conclusion

**CES is a high-value, legally mandated, long-running federal statistical program whose public importance extends far beyond the headline monthly jobs number.** Its strengths are timeliness, extensive industry coverage, a long historical record, administrative employment benchmarking, documented methods, and unrestricted reuse of public estimates.

Its principal limitations are scope exclusions, sampling and nonsampling uncertainty, changing classifications, earnings-composition effects, and substantial revision.

For preservation and responsible use, the central rule is:

> **Preserve the estimates, their metadata, and the version in which they were published.**

Without all three, one can describe today’s revised history—but not reliably reconstruct yesterday’s evidence.

# CES dataset risk assessment

**Assessment date: October 9, 2026**  
**Primary scope:** CES **national** data at https://www.bls.gov/ces/ and the national `CE` database. Changes to the related **state and metropolitan-area CES program** are identified separately.

## Overall finding

**CES remains available and operational, but continuity and institutional-independence risks are substantial.** Since January 2025, publication has been interrupted by funding lapses, some detailed national series have been discontinued or consolidated, and the President removed the BLS commissioner following an unfavorable jobs report.

The evidence is stronger for **publication disruption and loss of detail** than for wholesale deletion or deliberate falsification. I found no substantiated evidence that CES estimates have been politically fabricated.

These ratings apply your rubric to observed conditions since January 2025; they are **not numerical probabilities of future disappearance**. Where several levels have supporting evidence, I select the highest clearly established applicable trigger.

## 1. Historical Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — Not supported.** Historical national data remain publicly accessible. I retrieved the [total nonfarm employment bulk file](https://download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/ce/ce.data.00a.TotalNonfarm.Employment), which includes observations beginning in January 1939.
- **High Risk — Not established for the national database.** I did not verify removal of entire prior-year national data files. Discontinuing future publication of a series is not, by itself, proof that its historical observations have been deleted.
- **Moderate Risk — A significant concern, but historical removal is not verified nationally.** The [February 2025 national publication-change notice](https://www.bls.gov/ces/notices/2025/2025-bmk-series-changes.htm) documents discontinued and consolidated industry series. It also documents historical reconstruction and availability under replacement codes for certain changes. A before-and-after inventory is needed to establish which discontinued historical elements, if any, are no longer retrievable.
- **No Known Issue — Supported for the national historical holdings examined.**
  - Long-run national observations remain accessible.
  - BLS provides [CES vintage files](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesvindata.htm), preserving earlier published employment estimates—not merely today’s revised history.
  - [Vintage documentation](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesvininfo.htm) says these files contain published values beginning with the May 2003 release, with reference months extending back to 1939 for total nonfarm employment. Coverage includes employment at the 3-digit industry level and above.

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

**Why:** I verified substantial historical access and an official vintage repository, but did not establish national historical deletion. This is a qualified finding, not certification that every historical detailed series remains available.

I do **not** treat documented benchmarking, seasonal-adjustment revisions, or classification reconstruction as destructive alteration. They are normal statistical processes, and the vintage repository helps preserve the earlier estimates.

**Important state/area exception:** BLS explicitly announced that approximately **900 state/area employment, hours, and earnings series would no longer be available in its database** with January 2026 data. Its [benchmark article](https://www.bls.gov/sae/notices/2026/benchmark-article-2026.htm) confirms discontinuation. That is evidence of historical-access loss in the related product and warrants a separate elevated rating. It should not be silently attributed to the national database. - **High Risk — Supported by skipped publication.** BLS’s [official funding-lapse notice](https://www.bls.gov/bls/2025-lapse-revised-release-dates.htm) records:
  - September 2025 release delayed from **October 3 to November 20, 2025**.

Here, “quality” follows your rubric’s emphasis on **granularity, timeliness, and frequency**, rather than implying that every published estimate is inaccurate.

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — Not supported.** Collection and publication continue.
- **High Risk — Supported by actual reductions.**

## 4. Statutory Context

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — Not applicable.**
- **High Risk — Not supported.** CES has explicit legal authority and extensive documented uses. Related employment collections are not equivalent substitutes.
- **Moderate Risk — Not the best fit.** This is not merely a collection indirectly needed to administer another program.
- **No Known Issue — Strongly supported.**
  - **[29 U.S.C. § 2](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2)** directs BLS to collect and publish, **at least monthly**, employment, wages, and hours statistics, including specified government and industry coverage.
  - The [Federal Register CES notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/04/24/2024-08689/agency-information-collection-activities-submission-for-omb-review-report-on-current-employment) identifies CES as a Principal Federal Economic Indicator and a fundamental input for government, businesses, and organized labor.

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

**Why:** The statute clearly specifies the core subject matter and monthly publication requirement. CES also has deeply established policy and statistical uses.

**Limit:** The statute does not guarantee every detailed industry series, every historical version, or retention at a particular URL. Strong statutory protection for the core program does not eliminate preservation risk.

## Preservation implications

The priority is to protect **detailed series and release versions**, not just the headline employment total:

1. Archive national bulk files and metadata at each release.
2. Preserve official vintage files, release narratives, and benchmark documentation.
3. Independently investigate and recover discontinued state/area series.
4. Monitor ICR renewal before August 2027, enacted appropriations, staffing capacity, and any formal reorganization.
5. Preserve documented missing observations as missing; do not replace them with unlabeled estimates.

**Bottom line:** Complete national CES disappearance is not established or imminent on the evidence examined. Nevertheless, actual publication interruptions, reduced detail, and leadership removal justify urgent preservation work.
